questions.prompt: What does X do to a vector [alpha, beta]?
questions.explanation: Matrix multiplication by X exchanges the two entries. It swaps computational-basis probabilities as well as their amplitudes.

questions.prompt: Which gate leaves every input state unchanged?
questions.explanation: I is the identity transformation. Other gates can leave particular states unchanged, but not every state.

questions.prompt: Which relation defines an ideal unitary matrix U?

options.text: U times U always equals zero
U dagger times U equals I

questions.explanation: The dagger is conjugate transpose. This relation preserves vector length and makes U dagger the inverse.

options.text: It produces |-> without changing direct Z probabilities
It changes both amplitudes by the same sign

questions.explanation: Z negates the |1> amplitude only. The relative sign changes, while both squared magnitudes remain 1/2.

questions.prompt: Apply X to [sqrt(3)/2, i/2]. What are the resulting Z probabilities in order 0,1?
questions.explanation: X exchanges the amplitudes, giving [i/2, sqrt(3)/2]. Squared magnitudes are nonnegative, including for the imaginary entry.

questions.prompt: Using the displayed matrix for Y, what is Y|0>?
questions.explanation: Multiply Y by [1,0]: the result is [0,i]. The sign of i follows from the first column of Y.

questions.prompt: Starting from |0>, what state follows X and then H?
questions.explanation: X first gives |1>; H then gives |->. Operator notation writes this as HX|0>, with the rightmost gate acting first.

questions.prompt: Two paths prepare X then H, or H then X, from |0>. How does a final H and Z measurement distinguish them?

options.text: The first path yields 1 and the second yields 0
The first path yields 0 and the second yields 1

questions.explanation: Before the analyzer the states are |-> and |+>. Applying H converts their phase difference into opposite computational-basis outcomes.

questions.prompt: Why can an ideal unitary gate not reset both |0> and |1> to |0>?

options.text: That map loses input distinctions and cannot have a unitary inverse
All unitary matrices must exchange the basis states

questions.explanation: Unitary transformations preserve inner products and are reversible. Mapping two orthogonal inputs to one output violates those properties.

questions.prompt: What can be concluded from two adjacent Y gates in an ideal circuit, and what changes on hardware?

options.text: Y squared is X, so the bit always flips
Y squared destroys the relative phase permanently
The two physical operations are guaranteed to be noiseless
Y squared is I ideally, but physical execution may still add noise

questions.explanation: Multiplying the full matrices gives I for every input, including superpositions. Algebraic cancellation does not guarantee perfect physical gate implementations.
